summary:
Aguascalientes stands under the national framework of Mexico. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised and same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2009, but the state's own trans-specific legal provisions remain sparse.

Legal gender recognition in Mexico is determined state by state. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that only some states have reformed their legislation to create recognition procedures. Its state-by-state survey of 11 March 2025 records that Aguascalientes "has not reformed its legislation to create a legal gender recognition procedure for transgender people", which leaves the state without an administrative recognition mechanism of its own.

That gap was closed from the bench rather than the legislature. Infobae reported on 9 April 2026 that Mexico's Supreme Court, in Amparo en Revisión 430/2025 with a project by Minister Giovanni Figueroa Mejía, held the requirements of the Aguascalientes Civil Code for changing gender on birth certificates (judicial or ministerial intervention, civil trials, probative proof of identity, and marginal annotations) to be discriminatory and a violation of privacy. The Court ordered the state's Civil Registry to grant recognition through a simple, confidential administrative procedure honouring self-perception, with a new birth certificate issued and no marginal note revealing a prior gender. The ruling's immediate effect is limited to the persons represented by the civil association that filed the amparo, so a court-ordered recognition route now exists even though no legislative procedure is in force.

The absence of a state recognition procedure has documented consequences. The Human Rights Watch report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) set out how delays and refusals in name and gender recognition leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, with knock-on discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with the police; that report documented the situation in Tabasco, and non-reforming states including Aguascalientes face the same exposure.

Violence risk is not addressed by the ruling. La Jornada Aguascalientes reported on 23 August 2026 that activists Alicia Cruz, Kevin Cruz and Hened Musalem of Diversx Laboratorio Cultural Disidente say conversion-therapy operations still run in Aguascalientes under the guise of addiction-treatment annexes despite the legal prohibition, and that a person who escaped one of these spaces arrived at the group in the previous year. The same activists state that trans women continue to suffer prejudice-motivated aggression.

No transfemicide offence exists in Aguascalientes. The Guardian reported on 24 July 2024 that Mexico City made transfemicide a criminal offence, and Aguascalientes is one of the states that have adopted no comparable reform.
tangentialFactors:
The state sits inside a national pattern of partial reform. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that legal gender recognition is administered state by state and that implementation differs sharply between them, and warned that where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

Killings of trans people continue nationally. Transgender Europe monitoring recorded 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a total second only to Brazil's 100. The Associated Press reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, including activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, which prompted street demonstrations. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that violence against trans people and the murder of LGBTI+ defenders had risen over the previous year.

Regional oversight has intensified. In 2024 the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded investigation of all LGBTI violations using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may reach alarming levels. Analysis by Caroline Beer on the LSE USAPP blog (22 November 2024) found that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice.

The comparative reference point for punitive reform is Mexico City, whose Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished. Aguascalientes has not followed it.
localsOnly:
Residents of Aguascalientes can in principle obtain recognition of gender on their birth certificates through the state Civil Registry, following the Supreme Court's order that recognition be granted by a simple, confidential administrative procedure based on self-perception, with a new certificate issued and no marginal annotation recording a previous gender. Before that order, the Civil Code required judicial or ministerial intervention, civil trials, probative proof of identity and marginal annotations.

The reach of that order at present extends to the people represented by the civil association that brought the amparo. Others seeking recognition in Aguascalientes have no statutory procedure to apply under, since the state legislature has not reformed the Civil Code.

Conversion therapy is prohibited in Aguascalientes, but local activists say operations persist by presenting themselves as addiction-treatment annexes, and that at least one person who escaped such a space approached Diversx Laboratorio Cultural Disidente during 2025. The same activists report continuing prejudice-motivated aggression against trans women in the state.

Aguascalientes has no transfemicide-specific offence, so killings of trans people fall to be prosecuted as ordinary homicide. On demographic scale, the ENDISEG survey shows 7.3% of the state's population aged 15 and over self-identifies as LGBTI+, the fifth-highest proportion among Mexican states.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Supreme Court-ordered administrative route is now available to any resident of Aguascalientes, rather than only to the amparo plaintiffs, is unresolved in the sources available here; the reporting of 9 April 2026 describes the immediate effect as limited to the represented persons.

No source in this inventory records the status of legislative reform in the Aguascalientes Congress on legal gender recognition, nor any pending bill.

Aguascalientes-specific figures for killings of trans people, and any state-level hate-crime designation covering anti-trans violence, are not sourced here. National monitoring totals are cited as national figures only.

The claim that conversion-therapy operations continue in Aguascalientes rests on statements by named activists and the account of one person who left such a space; no inspection record, prosecution or regulator finding is available to corroborate enforcement of the prohibition.

The ENDISEG 7.3% figure and its ranking are reported without survey methodology or sampling detail in this inventory.
